video.title: Ethics, safe labs and assessment: Teaching attack without causing harm

chapters.label: A scan that went too far

scenes.narration: A keen student practised a network scan from the course on the university's live network. Within minutes, the security team had disabled his account and called our department.
Today: the ethics of teaching offensive skills, how to build an isolated lab, and how to assess students with capture-the-flag tasks and write-ups.

The same scan is a lesson in a lab and an offence on someone else's network. Many countries criminalise unauthorised access. So teaching offensive skills requires written authorisation, a defined scope, and an isolated environment.

Before the first offensive lab, students sign a short code of conduct. It names the lab networks they may test, forbids everything else, explains responsible disclosure, and states the consequences of breaking it.
A safe lab can run on one server: virtual machines on a host-only network, no route to the internet or the campus, and snapshots so any machine can be reset in seconds.

In a capture-the-flag task, each challenge hides a secret string. Finding it proves the technique worked. Flags are easy to auto-grade, but they can be shared, so the write-up carries most of the marks.
Every attack lab should end with defence. After exploiting a flaw, students write the fix, a detection rule, and a short note for a manager. That pairing builds professionals, not just attackers.
Quick check! The student scanned the live network. What should the course have provided to prevent this?
A signed scope that named the only allowed targets, and an isolated lab where practising was safe. The student needed a place to practise and clear limits.
In the app, open the phishing lab. Inspect each message for the signs of a phish, then discuss how you would run a phishing exercise ethically, with consent and no shaming.
Your turn. Flags from your last exercise appeared on a public forum. What change to the assessment protects its validity?
Per-student flags and graded write-ups. Remember: authorise and scope every offensive task, isolate the lab, and pair every attack with defence.
Try it this term: write a one-page code of conduct for your offensive labs. Review it with your university's IT security team before students sign it.

checkpoints.prompt: A student scanned the live campus network. What should the course have provided?

options.text: A signed scope and an isolated lab

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: clear limits and a safe place to practise prevent most incidents.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: removing practice doesn't build skill; scope and isolation make practice safe.

checkpoints.prompt: Flags from your exercise appeared online. Which change protects the assessment?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: unique flags and write-ups make shared answers useless.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: you can't control the internet, but you can design an assessment that copying doesn't satisfy.
